**Clerk — the ANALYZE that decided a column was entirely null (2026)**

Clerk sells hosted authentication, so when its API degrades, every sign-in on every customer's site degrades with it. The company's published postmortem for 19 February 2026 records the incident opening at 16:15 UTC, with over 95% of traffic returning 429s and the small remainder reaching the database and answering very slowly. Nothing had been deployed. The database was saturated by a query that had been running fine for months.

The cause was Postgres' automatic ANALYZE. One column in the affected table is null in 99.9996% of rows. Clerk's write-up describes the planner relying on "a sampling system to estimate data distribution"; when autoanalyze ran, "the planner's sample size was too low and it only found NULL values, which led it to erroneously conclude that 100% of the values were NULL." With a null fraction of exactly one, the estimate for the non-null predicate collapses to zero rows, and the planner chose the plan that is cheapest when nothing matches. Over 17,000 rows matched. Run at Clerk's request rate, that traversal consumed nearly all database resources.

Note what this is not. The statistics were not stale — they were fresh, and freshly wrong. ANALYZE, the reflex fix for a bad estimate, was the trigger. The plan was internally coherent: the executor did what a sensible plan for an empty result set does. And the estimated-versus-actual gap this lesson teaches you to hunt for in EXPLAIN ANALYZE was not tenfold or hundredfold, it was zero against seventeen thousand, which is the shape a sampled statistic produces on a long-tailed column.

Diagnosis cost most of the outage. The first thirty-five minutes went to a plausible wrong theory — a customer traffic spike — made more convincing by that customer's aggressive retry logic, which was itself a response to Clerk's failures. The team reached autoanalyze at 17:25; a manual ANALYZE at 17:27 restored the earlier plan and recovery began; stability was confirmed at 18:06. Afterwards they raised the statistics target on the table, refactored the query "so the planner could take a deterministic approach", and started auditing other queries for the same exposure.

When you read a plan in this lesson, the number to distrust first is the estimated row count on a selective predicate over a skewed column, because that is the estimate a sample can get catastrophically rather than marginally wrong. Decide in advance which queries you are content to leave at the planner's discretion, and treat a routine ANALYZE on a skewed table as what it is: a production change with no change ticket.

**Heap — ten million partial indexes, and the bill for building them (2017–2021)**

Heap captures every event on a customer's site and lets analysts define events retroactively, which means the filters are unknown at write time. Indexing every field of an event table measured in hundreds of terabytes would be ruinous, so Heap indexes the definitions instead: each defined event becomes a partial index of the form CREATE INDEX ON events (time) WHERE type = 'click' AND text = 'login'. Their 2017 engineering post reports over ten million such indexes in production, a figure later put at roughly thirty million. Tables are sharded so each holds one customer's data, so no single table carries more than a few thousand.

The economics are the ones this lesson describes, pushed to the limit. A defined event is typically a few per cent of raw events, so the partial index is a fraction of the size of indexing the underlying fields and takes maintenance writes on a fraction of inserts. What Heap gave up is write-path CPU. Every incoming event must be tested against every predicate on its table — thousands of them, including regular expressions over CSS selectors — so the bottleneck moves off disk and onto the processor, and it grows with the number of definitions rather than the number of rows.

The second cost is build time, and it is where the strategy nearly breaks. Postgres permits one CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY per table at a time, so concurrent builds serialise; each takes several times longer than an ordinary build, and a single long-running query blocks all of them. Heap's answer was to abandon concurrency: use plain CREATE INDEX and defer that customer's event writes for the duration. Building the full set for a large customer took a full day, limited by CPU rather than I/O.

In September 2021 they published the failure. Rolling one new index across every shard meant creating over a million indexes, and the planned rollout was not what hurt — the ambient work was. Customers creating event types triggered ordinary index-sync workers at the same time, and the combined load pushed ingestion latency, normally a minute or two, well past it. The fix was scheduling rather than indexing: mark backfill-only indexes so that only the workers spun up for a rollout will sync them.

Partial indexes are the cheapest item in this lesson on the storage line and among the most expensive on the operational one. Before you add the next index — partial, composite or covering — price the predicate against every insert, work out how the build completes without stopping writes, and find out which other process on that table is already queueing for the same lock.

**GitHub — forty-three seconds of partition, twenty-four hours of degradation (2018)**

On 21 October 2018 at 22:52 UTC, routine replacement of failing 100G optical equipment severed connectivity between GitHub's US East Coast network hub and its primary East Coast data centre. GitHub's published post-incident analysis states the link was restored in 43 seconds. The degradation lasted until 23:03 UTC the following day: 24 hours and 11 minutes, from under a minute of network loss.

The mechanism was the failover automation working as designed. GitHub used Orchestrator to manage MySQL topology, with Raft for consensus. During the partition the Orchestrator nodes inside the isolated primary data centre deselected leadership, while nodes in the West Coast data centre and the East Coast public cloud formed a quorum and failed clusters over so that writes went west. In those seconds, the East Coast primaries had accepted writes that never replicated — one busy cluster had 954 writes in the affected window.

When the link came back, both regions held writes the other lacked. That is the trap: failing back to the East Coast would have discarded newer West Coast writes, and staying put stranded the East Coast ones. GitHub chose to keep the West Coast primaries, which meant every write from East Coast application servers now crossed the country, and to rebuild the East Coast replicas from backups. Restoring terabyte-scale backups and then resynchronising the topology is what turned a network event into a day of stale and inconsistent data, absent webhooks and paused internal services.

The remediation is instructive because it removed capability rather than adding it: Orchestrator was reconfigured so it cannot promote primaries across regional boundaries. They also moved to component-level status reporting instead of a single global status, accelerated an active/active/active data centre design, and adopted deliberate fault injection.

This is the bargain in every automated failover you configure alongside your read replicas. Automation buys you seconds of recovery and pays for it with the risk of divergence, and divergence is settled in hours of reconciliation, not seconds of downtime. Before you enable cross-region promotion, answer GitHub's questions on your own topology: what is the blast radius of a promotion that is locally correct and globally wrong, are your replicas semi-synchronous enough to bound the lost window, and how would you find your equivalent of those 954 writes?

**Post Office — an append-only ledger the branch did not control (1999–2019)**

Horizon is an event-sourced accounting system in everything but name. Each branch's terminal emitted transactions to a central store, that store was treated as the authoritative record, and a branch's accounts were a projection over it. Its immutability was not an engineering nicety — it was the evidence. More than 900 subpostmasters were prosecuted between 1999 and 2015 on the strength of shortfalls the log appeared to prove, and the Post Office maintained for years that branch data could not be altered from outside the branch.

Mr Justice Fraser's Horizon Issues judgment of 16 December 2019 found otherwise: Horizon contained bugs, errors and defects capable of producing discrepancies in branch accounts, and Fujitsu could reach into those accounts. Evidence disclosed to the subsequent public inquiry describes a designed facility by which the Software Support Centre injects a transaction into a branch's stream — a "balancing transaction" — to correct a discrepancy, and which did not require the subpostmaster's acceptance in the way ordinary transaction types did. Appends were possible from an actor the projection could not distinguish from the branch itself.

The read-model failure is equally recognisable. Fujitsu's internal notes on the Receipts and Payments Mismatch issue, which began in September 2010 on Horizon Online, describe a sequence in which a branch cancelled completion of a trading period and then rolled into a new balancing period within the same session: the discrepancy vanished from the counter while remaining in the back-end branch account. The notes put it at circa 40 branches and circa £20,000. The operator's read model and the authoritative account disagreed, and the operator had no access to the stream being used against them.

Neither failure required anyone to run an UPDATE. That is the part worth sitting with. An append-only store can be perfectly append-only and still misrepresent reality, because "the log is immutable" is a claim about who may append and whether each append is attributable, not merely about the absence of destructive statements.

This is why the metadata column in your event schema carries as much weight as the payload. Every event needs an actor, a correlation id and a provenance that survives replay, so that an operational correction is legible as a correction rather than indistinguishable from an original fact. And whenever a projection is the thing a human is held accountable to, they need a route back to the events behind it — otherwise you have built a system that can be wrong in a way its users cannot argue with.

**Foursquare — the shard that outgrew its memory, and the fix that would not take (2010)**

In October 2010 Foursquare's check-in data lived in MongoDB across two shards, each on a machine with 66 GB of RAM, keyed on user id and split into 200 chunks. By count, the distribution was even. By load it was not: as the MongoDB team's public post-mortem of the outage explains, some users check in far more than others, so their writes concentrated. Over about two months one shard grew to roughly 67 GB while the other sat near 50 GB. The moment the working set stopped fitting in memory, reads and writes went to disk, latency collapsed and the site went down. TechCrunch reported the outage at approximately eleven hours on 4 October 2010.

The interesting part is the remedy. Adding a third shard and migrating around 5% of the data off the hot shard is the textbook move, and it did not work. Check-in documents are around 300 bytes, so removing 5% of them removed a scattering of tiny records from across the data files rather than freeing whole pages; the fragmented pages still had to be read into memory, and the shard's RAM requirement barely moved. The site stayed down while the obvious fix failed to bite.

What finally worked was offline compaction: taking the shard down and running repairDatabase(), which took about four hours and reclaimed enough space that the working set fit again. In other words, the escape route from a shard past its memory cliff was an operation that required the shard to be unavailable — precisely what you cannot afford during an outage caused by that shard.

Two lessons sit inside that. The shard key was not wrong in the hashing sense; it was wrong in the load sense, because it distributed rows evenly and activity unevenly. And headroom on a memory-resident working set is not a gradual quantity — the system is fine, then it is not, with no useful warning in the throughput graph beforehand.

When you pick a shard key in this lesson, model the distribution of writes and of hot reads rather than the distribution of rows, and be explicit about what your per-shard cliff actually is: RAM for the working set, IOPS, connection count or WAL throughput. Then rehearse the recovery. If your only route back from a saturated shard is an offline compaction, a resilvering or a rebalance that competes with live traffic, you have a scaling strategy with no reverse gear.
